$comment: Threads plan Part B: connections inside the New Testament, one book per PR, each draft until the owner approves it. Every connection states its order (older end, use, basis).

connections.label: The first book, to Theophilus
connections.explanation: Acts 1:1–3 names Luke 1:1–4: Acts opens by addressing Theophilus again and calling the Gospel its first book. Luke's prologue promised Theophilus an ordered account drawn from eyewitnesses; Acts sums that book up as what Jesus began to do and teach until he was taken up. The two prefaces make the Gospel and Acts one work in two volumes.

connections.label: The ascension told twice
connections.explanation: Acts 1:4–12 retells Luke 24:49–53: the second volume begins where the first ended, with the command to wait in Jerusalem for the Father's promise and Jesus taken up near the city. The Gospel closes at Bethany with a blessing and the disciples returning in joy; Acts adds the forty days, the cloud and the two men in white. Luke tells the same parting as an ending and as a beginning.

connections.label: Water and the Holy Spirit
connections.explanation: Acts 1:5 recalls Luke 3:16: before he is taken up, Jesus takes John the Baptist's contrast between baptism in water and baptism in the Holy Spirit and says it will come true within days. In the Gospel John spoke of one mightier than himself who would baptize with the Spirit and fire. Pentecost in the next chapter is told as that promise kept.

connections.label: Peter remembers the word
connections.explanation: Acts 11:16 recalls Luke 3:16: defending his visit to Cornelius in Jerusalem, Peter says he remembered the Lord's word about John baptizing in water and the coming baptism in the Spirit. That word goes back to John's own answer at the Jordan, taken up by Jesus before the ascension. Peter reads the Spirit falling on Gentiles as the same promise reaching them.

connections.label: Not worthy to untie his sandals
connections.explanation: Acts 13:24–25 quotes Luke 3:16: preaching in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, Paul recalls John the Baptist saying that one comes after him whose sandals he is not worthy to untie. The Gospel gives the saying at the Jordan, where John answers the crowds wondering whether he is the Christ. Paul uses it to present Jesus as the one John pointed to.

connections.label: Stephen dies as Jesus died
connections.explanation: Acts 7:59–60 echoes Luke 23:34–46: Stephen, stoned outside the city, commits his spirit to the Lord Jesus and asks that this sin not be held against his killers. On the cross in Luke, Jesus prays for forgiveness for those who do not know what they do and commends his spirit to the Father. Luke writes the first martyr's last words on the pattern of his Lord's.

connections.label: The eleven named again
connections.explanation: Acts 1:13 echoes Luke 6:12–16: after the ascension Acts lists the apostles gathered in the upper room, the same names Luke gave when Jesus chose the twelve after a night of prayer. Judas Iscariot, named last in the Gospel as the one who became a traitor, is missing from the second list. The gap is filled later in the chapter when Matthias is chosen.

connections.label: Get up: Jairus's daughter and Tabitha
connections.explanation: Acts 9:36–42 echoes Luke 8:49–56: at Joppa Peter sends everyone out of the room, prays, and tells the dead Tabitha to get up, and she opens her eyes and sits up. Peter had been one of the few Jesus let into the house of Jairus, where he put the mourners outside and told the dead girl to arise. Luke tells the disciple's miracle in the shape of the master's.

connections.label: The Lord's Prayer in two Gospels
connections.explanation: Matthew 6:9–13 and Luke 11:2–4 both tell the prayer Jesus taught: the Father's name kept holy, the Kingdom, daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from temptation and the evil one. Matthew sets it in the Sermon on the Mount; Luke gives it when a disciple asks to be taught to pray, in a shorter form. Luke speaks of sins where Matthew speaks of debts.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Matthew and Luke wrote independently, each drawing on Mark and a shared collection of sayings, while Augustine held that the Gospels were written in the order Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, so whether Luke knew Matthew is disputed.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: first Matthew, then Mark, thirdly Luke, lastly John

connections.label: Three temptations in the wilderness
connections.explanation: Matthew 4:1–11 and Luke 4:1–13 both tell of Jesus tempted by the devil for forty days in the wilderness and answering each temptation from Deuteronomy. Bread from stones, the kingdoms of the world and the leap from the temple come in both, but Luke puts the temple last, so his account ends in Jerusalem. Luke adds that the devil left him until another time.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Matthew and Luke wrote independently, each drawing on Mark and a shared collection of sayings, while Augustine held that the Gospels were written in the order Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, so whether Luke knew Matthew is disputed.

connections.label: The Transfiguration
connections.explanation: Luke 9:28–36 retells Mark 9:2–8: Jesus is changed before Peter, James and John on a mountain, with Moses and Elijah, a cloud and a voice naming him the beloved Son. Luke adds that Jesus was praying and that the three spoke of the departure he would accomplish at Jerusalem. Both end with Jesus alone.

connections.label: The Beatitudes
connections.explanation: Matthew 5:3–12 and Luke 6:20–23 both tell the blessings that open Jesus' great sermon: on the poor, the hungry, those who mourn or weep, and those reviled for his sake, like the prophets before them. Matthew has nine on a mountain and speaks of the poor in spirit; Luke has four on a level place, followed by four woes.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Matthew and Luke wrote independently, each drawing on Mark and a shared collection of sayings, while Augustine held that the Gospels were written in the order Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, so whether Luke knew Matthew is disputed.

connections.label: Two genealogies of Jesus
connections.explanation: Matthew 1:1–17 and Luke 3:23–38 both tell the descent of Jesus through Joseph, sharing the line from Abraham to David. Matthew runs forward from Abraham in three sets of fourteen and follows the kings through Solomon; Luke runs backward from Jesus through Nathan, David's son, to Adam and God. The two lists part between David and Joseph.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Matthew and Luke wrote independently, each drawing on Mark and a shared collection of sayings, while Augustine held that the Gospels were written in the order Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, so whether Luke knew Matthew is disputed.

connections.label: The annunciation to Joseph and to Mary
connections.explanation: Matthew 1:18–25 and Luke 1:26–38 both tell of a virgin betrothed to Joseph of David's line, the child conceived by the Holy Spirit, and an angel giving the name Jesus. Matthew tells it from Joseph's side, in a dream that stops him from sending Mary away; Luke tells it from Mary's, with Gabriel at Nazareth and her consent.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Matthew and Luke wrote independently, each drawing on Mark and a shared collection of sayings, while Augustine held that the Gospels were written in the order Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, so whether Luke knew Matthew is disputed.

sources.phrase: first Matthew, then Mark, thirdly Luke, lastly John

connections.label: Born in Bethlehem
connections.explanation: Matthew 2:1 and Luke 2:1–7 both tell that Jesus was born at Bethlehem in Judea, David's town. Matthew dates it to the days of King Herod and moves on to the wise men; Luke brings Joseph and Mary from Nazareth for Augustus's census and lays the child in a manger. Neither account names the other's reason for Bethlehem.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Matthew and Luke wrote independently, each drawing on Mark and a shared collection of sayings, while Augustine held that the Gospels were written in the order Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, so whether Luke knew Matthew is disputed.

sources.phrase: first Matthew, then Mark, thirdly Luke, lastly John

connections.label: Rejected at Nazareth
connections.explanation: Luke 4:16–30 retells Mark 6:1–6: Jesus teaches in his home town's synagogue on the Sabbath, the people take offence at one they knew, and he says a prophet is not honoured in his own country. Luke moves the scene to the start of the ministry and has Jesus read from Isaiah; there the town tries to throw him from a cliff.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament

connections.label: The parable of the sower
connections.explanation: Luke 8:4–15 retells Mark 4:1–20: Jesus tells of seed falling on the road, the rock, among thorns and in good soil, and explains it to the disciples as the word heard in four ways. Mark sets Jesus in a boat by the sea; Luke has a crowd from every town. Luke's good soil holds the word fast with an honest heart and bears fruit with patience.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: chapter 6, the Synoptic Problem (the priority of Mark)

connections.label: Who do you say that I am?
connections.explanation: Luke 9:18–22 retells Mark 8:27–31: Jesus asks who people say he is, Peter names him the Christ, and Jesus orders silence and first says that the Son of Man must suffer. Mark places it near Caesarea Philippi; Luke sets it while Jesus prays alone.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: chapter 6, the Synoptic Problem (the priority of Mark)

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: first Matthew, then Mark, thirdly Luke, lastly John

connections.label: The Last Supper
connections.explanation: Luke 22:14–20 retells Mark 14:22–25: at the supper Jesus breaks bread as his body, gives the cup of the covenant in his blood, and vows not to drink of the vine again until the Kingdom. Luke has two cups, one before the bread and one after supper, and adds the command to do this in memory of him.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: chapter 6, the Synoptic Problem (the priority of Mark)

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: first Matthew, then Mark, thirdly Luke, lastly John

connections.label: The death of Jesus
connections.explanation: Luke 23:44–49 retells Mark 15:33–41: darkness falls from the sixth to the ninth hour, the temple veil is torn, Jesus cries out and dies, and a centurion speaks while women watch from afar. In Mark Jesus cries the opening of Psalm 22 and the centurion calls him God's Son; in Luke he commends his spirit to the Father and the centurion calls him righteous.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: chapter 6, the Synoptic Problem (the priority of Mark)

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: first Matthew, then Mark, thirdly Luke, lastly John

connections.label: The women at the empty tomb
connections.explanation: Luke 24:1–11 retells Mark 16:1–8: the women come with spices at dawn on the first day of the week, find the stone rolled away and the body gone, and hear that Jesus is risen. Mark has one young man in white and women who flee and say nothing; Luke has two men in dazzling clothes and women who tell the eleven, who do not believe them.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: chapter 6, the Synoptic Problem (the priority of Mark)

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: first Matthew, then Mark, thirdly Luke, lastly John

connections.label: The lost sheep
connections.explanation: Matthew 18:12–14 and Luke 15:3–7 both tell the parable of the man with a hundred sheep who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one that went astray and rejoices over it. In Matthew it teaches care for the little ones within the community; in Luke it answers those who grumble that Jesus eats with sinners, and ends in joy in heaven over one who repents.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Matthew and Luke wrote independently, each drawing on Mark and a shared collection of sayings, while Augustine held that the Gospels were written in the order Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, so whether Luke knew Matthew is disputed.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: first Matthew, then Mark, thirdly Luke, lastly John

connections.label: Martha and Mary
connections.explanation: Luke 10:38–42 and John 11:1–5 both tell of the sisters Martha and Mary as friends of Jesus. In Luke Martha is busy serving while Mary sits at his feet listening; in John they live at Bethany with their brother Lazarus, and send word when he falls sick. John's chapter keeps the pattern, with Martha going out to meet Jesus while Mary stays in the house.

connections.label: Two men named Lazarus
connections.explanation: Luke 16:19–31 is set against John 11:38–44: in Jesus' parable Abraham says that those who will not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead. In John a man of the same name, Lazarus of Bethany, is called out of his tomb after four days. The chapter goes on to show some believing and the council resolving to kill Jesus.

connections.label: Peter runs to the tomb
connections.explanation: Luke 24:12 and John 20:3–10 both tell of Peter running to the tomb, stooping to look in, and seeing the linen cloths lying there before going home. John has a second disciple outrun Peter, and Peter go into the tomb and see the head cloth rolled up apart. In Luke Peter leaves wondering; in John the other disciple sees and believes.

connections.label: A night without fish, then the nets full
connections.explanation: Luke 5:1–11 and John 21:1–11 both tell of Simon Peter and his partners fishing all night and catching nothing, until Jesus tells them where to let down the nets and the catch is too great to haul. In Luke it comes at the call of the first disciples on the lake of Gennesaret; in John it comes after the resurrection at the sea of Tiberias, where Jesus waits on the shore.

connections.label: Peace be to you
connections.explanation: Luke 24:36–43 and John 20:19–23 both tell of the risen Jesus standing among the disciples on the evening of the first day, greeting them with peace and showing them his wounds. Luke has them think he is a spirit until he eats a piece of fish before them; John has him breathe on them and give them the Holy Spirit and authority to forgive sins.

connections.label: Five thousand fed
connections.explanation: Luke 9:10–17 and John 6:1–14 both tell of Jesus feeding five thousand men with five loaves and two fish, the people made to sit down and twelve baskets of pieces left over. Luke places it near Bethsaida after the apostles return; John puts it on a mountain across the sea near Passover, names Philip and Andrew and a boy with barley loaves, and has the crowd call Jesus the prophet.

connections.label: A woman anoints his feet
connections.explanation: Luke 7:36–50 and John 12:1–8 both tell of a woman at a meal who anoints Jesus' feet with costly ointment and wipes them with her hair. In Luke she is a sinner in the house of Simon the Pharisee, and Jesus answers his host with a parable of two debtors and forgives her; in John she is Mary of Bethany, Judas objects, and Jesus speaks of his burial.

connections.label: The arrest and the servant's ear
connections.explanation: Luke 22:47–53 and John 18:1–11 both tell of Judas bringing an armed party to take Jesus, and a disciple cutting off the right ear of the high priest's servant. Luke has Judas come to kiss Jesus and Jesus heal the ear; John names Peter and the servant Malchus, and has the soldiers fall back when Jesus says he is the one they seek.

connections.label: Before Pilate
connections.explanation: Luke 23:1–25 and John 18:28–19:16 both tell of Pilate asking Jesus if he is the King of the Jews, finding no basis for a charge, and giving in to a crowd that demands Barabbas and a crucifixion. Luke adds the hearing before Herod and Pilate's three declarations of innocence; John gives the dialogue about kingship and truth inside the Praetorium.

connections.label: This is my body: the Gospel and Paul
connections.explanation: Luke 22:19–20 and 1 Corinthians 11:23–25 both tell the words over the bread and cup on the night Jesus was betrayed: his body, the new covenant in his blood, and the command to do this in his memory. Paul hands it on to the Corinthians as received from the Lord. Luke and Paul agree closely here, against Mark and Matthew, in the cup after supper.

connections.label: The laborer is worthy of his wages
connections.explanation: Luke 10:7 and 1 Timothy 5:18 both tell the saying that a laborer deserves his pay. In Luke Jesus says it when he sends out the seventy, to let them stay and eat where they are received; in First Timothy it follows a line from Deuteronomy about the ox treading grain, both brought in as Scripture to argue that elders who teach should be paid.

connections.label: Let down the wall in a basket
connections.explanation: 2 Corinthians 11:32–33 and Acts 9:23–25 both tell of Paul escaping Damascus by night, let down through the city wall in a basket. Paul blames the governor under King Aretas, who guarded the city to seize him, and counts the flight among his humiliations; Acts says the Jews plotted to kill him and watched the gates, and his disciples lowered him.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Acts and on the undisputed letters of Paul (date of writing)

connections.label: Once I was stoned
connections.explanation: 2 Corinthians 11:25 and Acts 14:19–20 both tell of Paul being stoned. In the list of his sufferings Paul says he was stoned once; Acts tells of it at Lystra, where Jews from Antioch and Iconium won over the crowd, and Paul was dragged out of the city as dead before he got up and went back in.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Acts and on the undisputed letters of Paul (date of writing)

connections.label: Shamefully treated at Philippi
connections.explanation: 1 Thessalonians 2:2 and Acts 16:19–24 both tell of the harm Paul suffered at Philippi before he came to Thessalonica. Paul reminds the Thessalonians that he had been shamefully treated there and still spoke boldly; Acts tells how he and Silas were dragged before the magistrates, beaten with rods and put in the stocks.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Acts and on the undisputed letters of Paul (date of writing)

connections.label: Prisca and Aquila
connections.explanation: Romans 16:3–4 and Acts 18:1–3 both tell of the couple Aquila and Prisca, or Priscilla, as Paul's fellow workers. Paul greets them as having risked their necks for his life; Acts tells how he met them at Corinth after Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome, lodged with them and worked with them at their trade of tent making.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Acts and on the undisputed letters of Paul (date of writing)

connections.label: Apollos waters
connections.explanation: 1 Corinthians 3:4–6 and Acts 18:24–28 both tell of Apollos following Paul at Corinth. Paul tells the Corinthians, divided between his name and Apollos's, that he planted, Apollos watered and God gave the growth; Acts introduces Apollos as an eloquent Alexandrian, taught more exactly by Priscilla and Aquila, who went on to Achaia and helped the believers there.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Acts and on the undisputed letters of Paul (date of writing)

connections.label: A Pharisee
connections.explanation: Philippians 3:5 and Acts 23:6 both tell that Paul was a Pharisee. In Philippians he lists it among the credentials he now counts as loss for Christ; in Acts he cries it out before the council, a son of Pharisees on trial for the hope of the resurrection, and divides the Pharisees from the Sadducees.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Acts and on the undisputed letters of Paul (date of writing)

connections.label: Zealous for the traditions
connections.explanation: Galatians 1:14 and Acts 22:3 both tell of Paul's zeal in his former life. In Galatians he says he outstripped others of his age in Judaism, zealous for the traditions of his fathers; in Acts, speaking to the crowd in Jerusalem, he says he was raised there at the feet of Gamaliel in the strict law of the fathers.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Acts and on the undisputed letters of Paul (date of writing)

connections.label: Paul's first visit to Jerusalem
connections.explanation: Galatians 1:18–24 and Acts 9:26–30 both tell of Paul going up to Jerusalem after his turning and then leaving for Syria and Cilicia. Galatians says he went after three years, saw only Peter and James for fifteen days, and swears to it; Acts says Barnabas brought him to the apostles, he preached boldly, and the believers sent him off to Tarsus.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Acts and on the undisputed letters of Paul (date of writing)

connections.label: The meeting in Jerusalem
connections.explanation: Galatians 2:1–10 and Acts 15:1–29 both tell of Paul and Barnabas going up to Jerusalem over whether Gentile believers must be circumcised, and of Peter and James siding with them. Galatians stresses a private meeting and the request to remember the poor; Acts gives a public assembly and a letter. Whether the two tell the same visit is itself debated.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Acts and on the undisputed letters of Paul (date of writing)

connections.label: He appeared to me also
connections.explanation: 1 Corinthians 15:8 and Acts 9:3–6 both tell of the risen Jesus appearing to Paul. In First Corinthians Paul lists himself last among the witnesses, as one untimely born; Acts tells it as a light from heaven on the road to Damascus and a voice asking Saul why he persecutes him.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Acts and on the undisputed letters of Paul (date of writing)

connections.label: Sent to the Gentiles
connections.explanation: Galatians 1:15–16 and Acts 26:16–18 both tell that Paul's call was a commission to the Gentiles. Galatians says God, who set him apart from birth, revealed his Son in him so that he would preach him among the nations; in Acts, before Agrippa, Paul gives the words of the risen Jesus sending him to open their eyes and turn them from darkness to light.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Acts and on the undisputed letters of Paul (date of writing)

connections.label: Justified apart from the law
connections.explanation: Romans 3:28 and Acts 13:38–39 both tell that a person is justified through faith and not by the law. Romans states it as the conclusion of Paul's argument; in Acts it is the close of his first recorded sermon, at Pisidian Antioch, offering forgiveness through Jesus to everyone who believes.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Acts and on the undisputed letters of Paul (date of writing)

connections.label: The field of blood
connections.explanation: Matthew 27:3–8 and Acts 1:18–19 both tell of Judas's death and a field near Jerusalem called the field of blood. In Matthew he throws the silver into the temple and hangs himself, and the priests buy a potter's field with the money; in Acts he buys a field himself and falls headlong. The two accounts differ, but agree on the name.

connections.label: False witnesses about the temple
connections.explanation: Mark 14:57–58 and Acts 6:13–14 both tell of false witnesses claiming to have heard that Jesus would destroy the temple. At Jesus' trial they quote him as promising to build another not made with hands; at Stephen's they accuse him of saying Jesus would destroy this place and change the customs of Moses. Stephen's trial follows his Lord's.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: chapter 6, the Synoptic Problem (the priority of Mark)

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: first Matthew, then Mark, thirdly Luke, lastly John

connections.label: The cup James would drink
connections.explanation: Mark 10:38–39 and Acts 12:1–2 both tell what became of James, the son of Zebedee. When James and John asked for the places of honour, Jesus told them they would drink his cup and share his baptism; Acts records in one line that Herod killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: chapter 6, the Synoptic Problem (the priority of Mark)

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: first Matthew, then Mark, thirdly Luke, lastly John

connections.label: All foods clean
connections.explanation: Mark 7:18–19 and Acts 10:9–16 both tell that the food laws no longer divide. Mark notes that Jesus' saying about what goes into a man made all foods clean; in Acts Peter, shown unclean animals in a vision, refuses to eat and hears that what God has cleansed he must not call common. The vision opens the way to Cornelius's house.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: chapter 6, the Synoptic Problem (the priority of Mark)

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: first Matthew, then Mark, thirdly Luke, lastly John

connections.label: John Mark
connections.explanation: Acts 12:12 and Colossians 4:10 both tell of the Mark who went with Paul and Barnabas. Acts names his mother Mary, whose house in Jerusalem Peter went to after his escape; Colossians calls him the cousin of Barnabas and says he is with Paul and should be welcomed.

connections.label: Mark, refused and asked for
connections.explanation: Acts 15:36–40 is set against 2 Timothy 4:11: Paul refuses to take Mark on a second journey because he left them in Pamphylia, and parts from Barnabas over it. In Second Timothy Paul asks Timothy to bring Mark with him, as useful for the ministry.

connections.label: Timothy's mother
connections.explanation: Acts 16:1–3 and 2 Timothy 1:5 both tell of Timothy's family. Acts says he was the son of a believing Jewish woman and a Greek father, and that Paul took him along from Lystra; Second Timothy names his mother Eunice and grandmother Lois, in whom his sincere faith lived first.

connections.label: Antioch, Iconium and Lystra
connections.explanation: Acts 14:19–20 and 2 Timothy 3:11 both tell of the persecutions Paul suffered at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra. Acts gives the story, ending in his stoning at Lystra by Jews from the other two cities; Second Timothy names the three places together and says the Lord rescued him from them all.

connections.label: The baptism of Jesus
connections.explanation: Matthew 3:13–17 and Mark 1:9–11 both tell of Jesus baptized by John in the Jordan, the Spirit coming down like a dove, and a voice from heaven naming him the beloved Son. Matthew adds John's protest that he needs to be baptized by Jesus. In Mark the voice speaks to Jesus himself; in Matthew it speaks of him to those present.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: Mark follows him closely, and looks like his attendant and epitomizer.

connections.label: Fishers of men
connections.explanation: Matthew 4:18–22 and Mark 1:16–20 both tell of Jesus calling Simon and Andrew from their nets to be fishers of men, then James and John from their father Zebedee's boat. All four leave at once. Mark adds that the brothers left their father in the boat with the hired servants.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: Mark follows him closely, and looks like his attendant and epitomizer.

connections.label: The paralysed man forgiven and healed
connections.explanation: Matthew 9:1–8 and Mark 2:1–12 both tell of a paralysed man whose sins Jesus forgives, the scribes' charge of blasphemy, and the healing that shows the Son of Man's authority. Mark has the friends open the roof and let the man down through it. Matthew ends with the crowds praising God for giving such authority to men.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: Mark follows him closely, and looks like his attendant and epitomizer.

connections.label: The storm stilled
connections.explanation: Matthew 8:23–27 and Mark 4:35–41 both tell of a great storm on the lake while Jesus sleeps, the disciples waking him in fear, his rebuke of the wind and sea, and their wonder at who he is. In Mark he sleeps on a cushion in the stern and they ask if he does not care that they are perishing. Matthew has Jesus reproach their little faith before he calms the sea.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown

connections.label: The demons sent into the pigs
connections.explanation: Matthew 8:28–34 and Mark 5:1–20 both tell of demons cast out among the tombs across the lake, sent into a herd of pigs that rushes into the sea, and the townspeople asking Jesus to leave. Matthew has two men; Mark has one, who gives his name as Legion, and tells of about two thousand pigs. Mark ends with the healed man telling his story in the Decapolis.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

connections.label: The death of John the Baptist
connections.explanation: Matthew 14:1–12 and Mark 6:14–29 both tell of Herod fearing that Jesus is John raised, and of John's death: imprisoned over Herodias and beheaded after her daughter danced for Herod. Mark tells it at greater length, adding that Herod feared John as a holy man and liked to listen to him. In Matthew John's disciples bury him and go to tell Jesus.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

connections.label: Five thousand fed
connections.explanation: Matthew 14:13–21 and Mark 6:30–44 both tell of Jesus moved with compassion for the crowd in a deserted place, five loaves and two fish blessed and broken, everyone fed and twelve baskets left. Mark adds that the people were like sheep without a shepherd and sat in groups on the green grass. Matthew counts five thousand men besides women and children.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

sources.phrase: Mark follows him closely, and looks like his attendant and epitomizer.

connections.label: Walking on the sea
connections.explanation: Matthew 14:22–33 and Mark 6:45–52 both tell of Jesus coming to the disciples across the sea in the night, their fear that he is a ghost, his word of comfort and the wind ceasing as he enters the boat. Matthew adds Peter walking on the water and sinking, and the disciples worshipping Jesus as the Son of God. Mark ends instead with their hearts hardened, not understanding about the loaves.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

connections.label: The crumbs under the table
connections.explanation: Matthew 15:21–28 and Mark 7:24–30 both tell of a Gentile woman near Tyre begging help for her daughter, Jesus' saying about the children's bread, and her answer that dogs eat the crumbs. Matthew calls her a Canaanite and has Jesus praise her great faith; Mark calls her a Syrophoenician Greek. In both her daughter is healed.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

connections.label: Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi
connections.explanation: Matthew 16:13–23 and Mark 8:27–33 both tell of Jesus asking at Caesarea Philippi who he is, Peter naming him the Christ, the first word of his suffering, and his rebuke of Peter as Satan. Matthew adds the Son of the living God, Jesus' blessing on Peter, the rock on which he will build his church, and the keys of the Kingdom.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

connections.label: The Transfiguration
connections.explanation: Matthew 17:1–8 and Mark 9:2–8 both tell of Jesus changed before Peter, James and John on a high mountain, with Moses and Elijah, and a voice from the cloud naming the beloved Son. Mark says his clothes were whiter than any launderer could make them; Matthew adds the disciples falling on their faces and Jesus touching them.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

connections.label: The rich man and the eye of a needle
connections.explanation: Matthew 19:16–30 and Mark 10:17–31 both tell of a rich man asking about eternal life, told to sell what he has and follow Jesus, going away sad, and the saying about a camel and the eye of a needle. Matthew calls him young; Mark says Jesus looked at him and loved him. Both end with a hundredfold reward and the first who will be last.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

sources.phrase: Mark follows him closely, and looks like his attendant and epitomizer.

connections.label: The entry into Jerusalem
connections.explanation: Matthew 21:1–11 and Mark 11:1–11 both tell of two disciples sent from Bethphage for a colt, garments and branches spread on the road, and crowds crying Hosanna as Jesus rides into Jerusalem. Mark has one colt that no one had ridden; Matthew has a donkey with her colt and quotes the prophet, in words from Zechariah. Matthew adds the city stirred and asking who he is.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament

sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: Mark follows him closely, and looks like his attendant and epitomizer.

connections.label: The great commandment
connections.explanation: Matthew 22:34–40 and Mark 12:28–34 both tell of a question about the greatest commandment and Jesus' answer: love God with all your heart, soul and mind, and your neighbour as yourself. In Matthew a lawyer asks to test him, and Jesus says the whole law and the prophets hang on these two. In Mark a scribe agrees, and Jesus tells him he is not far from the Kingdom.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: Mark follows him closely, and looks like his attendant and epitomizer.

connections.label: The discourse on the Mount of Olives
connections.explanation: Matthew 24:1–35 and Mark 13:1–31 both tell Jesus' words on the temple thrown down, wars, false christs, the abomination of desolation, and the Son of Man coming on the clouds. Both end with the fig tree and the saying that heaven and earth will pass away but his words will not. Matthew carries the discourse on with parables of readiness.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament

sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: Mark follows him closely, and looks like his attendant and epitomizer.

connections.label: Gethsemane
connections.explanation: Matthew 26:36–46 and Mark 14:32–42 both tell of Jesus praying in Gethsemane that the cup pass from him, yet as the Father wills, and finding Peter, James and John asleep three times. Both give his warning that the spirit is willing but the flesh weak. Mark keeps the Aramaic word Abba in his prayer.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: Mark follows him closely, and looks like his attendant and epitomizer.

connections.label: Peter's three denials
connections.explanation: Matthew 26:69–75 and Mark 14:66–72 both tell of Peter in the high priest's courtyard denying Jesus three times, the last with curses, and weeping when the rooster crows and he remembers Jesus' words. In Mark the rooster crows twice, as Jesus had foretold. Matthew says he went out and wept bitterly.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: Mark follows him closely, and looks like his attendant and epitomizer.

connections.label: The women at the tomb
connections.explanation: Matthew 28:1–8 and Mark 16:1–8 both tell of women coming to the tomb at dawn after the Sabbath, an angel's message that Jesus is risen and goes before them to Galilee, and the women leaving in fear. Matthew adds an earthquake, the angel rolling back the stone, and the women running with great joy to tell the disciples. Mark ends with them saying nothing to anyone.

order.note: Most modern scholars hold that Mark wrote first and Matthew used his Gospel, while Augustine held that Matthew wrote first and Mark followed him as an abridger, so which drew on which is disputed.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament

sources.author: Augustine
sources.heading: Chapter II.
sources.phrase: Mark follows him closely, and looks like his attendant and epitomizer.

connections.label: The household: wives, children, servants
connections.explanation: Ephesians 5:22–6:9 retells Colossians 3:18–4:1: wives and husbands, children and parents, servants and masters in that order, servants working as for the Lord and masters under a Master in heaven. Ephesians enlarges the word to husbands into Christ's love for the church, and quotes the commandment to honour father and mother.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapter on Ephesians (its relation to Colossians)

connections.label: The old self and the new
connections.explanation: Ephesians 4:22–24 echoes Colossians 3:9–10: the old self is put off and the new put on, renewed after God's likeness. Colossians speaks of a new self renewed in knowledge after its Creator's image; Ephesians speaks of being renewed in the spirit of the mind and of a new self created in righteousness and holiness.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapter on Ephesians (its relation to Colossians)

connections.label: Psalms, hymns and spiritual songs
connections.explanation: Ephesians 5:19–20 echoes Colossians 3:16–17: believers are to sing psalms, hymns and spiritual songs from the heart and give thanks to God in the name of the Lord Jesus. In Colossians the singing comes from Christ's word dwelling richly among them; in Ephesians it comes from being filled with the Spirit.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapter on Ephesians (its relation to Colossians)

connections.label: Tychicus carries the letter
connections.explanation: Ephesians 6:21–22 retells Colossians 4:7–8: both letters close by commending Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant, sent so that the readers may know how Paul is and be comforted. The two passages run almost word for word, one of the longest stretches of shared wording between two New Testament letters.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapter on Ephesians (its relation to Colossians)

connections.label: The head of the body, the church
connections.explanation: Ephesians 1:22–23 echoes Colossians 1:18: Christ is the head of the body, which is the church. Colossians adds that he is the beginning and the firstborn from the dead; Ephesians that God has put all things under his feet, and that the church is his fullness.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapter on Ephesians (its relation to Colossians)

connections.label: Fallen angels and Sodom
connections.explanation: 2 Peter 2:4–6 retells Jude 1:6–7: the angels who sinned are kept in darkness for the judgement, and Sodom and Gomorrah stand as an example of what comes to the ungodly. Jude speaks of angels who left their proper dwelling and of cities that suffer eternal fire; Second Peter adds Noah, preserved with seven others when the flood came on the ungodly.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapter on 2 Peter (its use of Jude)

connections.label: The way of Balaam
connections.explanation: 2 Peter 2:15–16 retells Jude 1:11: the false teachers have gone the way of Balaam, who loved the wages of wrongdoing. Jude sets Balaam beside Cain and Korah; Second Peter tells how a speechless donkey spoke with a man's voice and stopped the prophet's madness.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapter on 2 Peter (its use of Jude)

connections.label: Scoffers in the last days
connections.explanation: 2 Peter 3:2–3 retells Jude 1:17–18: readers are to remember what the apostles said beforehand, that scoffers would come in the last days following their own desires. Second Peter adds what the scoffers say, asking where the promise of his coming is.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapter on 2 Peter (its use of Jude)

connections.label: Abraham believed God
connections.explanation: Galatians 3:6–9 and Romans 4:1–3 both tell that Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness, quoting Genesis to show that righteousness comes through faith. Galatians draws from it that those of faith are Abraham's children and that the nations are blessed in him; Romans asks what Abraham gained and answers that it was not by works.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Paul's undisputed letters (their order and dates)

connections.label: Abba, Father
connections.explanation: Galatians 4:6–7 and Romans 8:15–17 both tell that the Spirit makes believers God's children, crying Abba, Father, and so heirs. Galatians says they are no longer slaves but sons; Romans adds that they are joint heirs with Christ, suffering with him so as to be glorified with him.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Paul's undisputed letters (their order and dates)

connections.label: The whole law in one word
connections.explanation: Galatians 5:14 and Romans 13:8–10 both tell that the law is fulfilled in one command, to love your neighbour as yourself. Romans names the commandments against adultery, murder, theft and coveting as summed up in it, and adds that love does no harm to a neighbour.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Paul's undisputed letters (their order and dates)

connections.label: Not by works of the law
connections.explanation: Galatians 2:16 and Romans 3:20–28 both tell that a person is put right with God through faith in Jesus Christ and not by doing what the law commands. In Galatians Paul says it to Peter at Antioch; in Romans it closes his argument that all have sinned and are justified freely by God's grace.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Paul's undisputed letters (their order and dates)

connections.label: One body with many members
connections.explanation: 1 Corinthians 12:12–27 and Romans 12:4–8 both tell that believers are one body in Christ with many members, each with its own gift. First Corinthians plays out the figure with the foot, the hand, the eye and the ear; Romans lists prophecy, serving, teaching, exhortation, giving, leading and mercy.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Paul's undisputed letters (their order and dates)

connections.label: Adam and Christ
connections.explanation: 1 Corinthians 15:20–22 and Romans 5:12–19 both tell of Adam and Christ as the two men through whom death and life came. First Corinthians says that as all die in Adam, all will be made alive in Christ; Romans sets one man's trespass against one man's obedience and the gift of grace.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Paul's undisputed letters (their order and dates)

connections.label: The trumpet and the raising of the dead
connections.explanation: 1 Thessalonians 4:15–17 and 1 Corinthians 15:51–52 both tell that at the sound of the trumpet the dead will be raised and those still living will not be left behind. First Thessalonians says the living will be caught up with them in the clouds to meet the Lord; First Corinthians that all will be changed in the twinkling of an eye.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Paul's undisputed letters (their order and dates)

connections.label: The armour of God
connections.explanation: 1 Thessalonians 5:8 and Ephesians 6:13–17 both tell of the believer armed for the fight, with a breastplate and the hope of salvation for a helmet. First Thessalonians names the breastplate faith and love; Ephesians gives the whole armour, with truth as a belt, righteousness as a breastplate, faith as a shield and the word of God as the Spirit's sword.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Paul's undisputed letters (their order and dates)

connections.label: A new creation
connections.explanation: 2 Corinthians 5:17 and Galatians 6:15 both tell that in Christ there is a new creation. Second Corinthians adds that the old things have passed away; Galatians says that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only the new creation.

connections.label: A Hebrew of Hebrews
connections.explanation: 2 Corinthians 11:22 and Philippians 3:4–6 both tell Paul's own descent when others boast of theirs: a Hebrew, an Israelite, of Abraham's line. Philippians adds his circumcision on the eighth day, his tribe of Benjamin, his life as a Pharisee and a persecutor, and then counts all of it as loss for Christ.

connections.label: The words over the bread and cup
connections.explanation: 1 Corinthians 11:23–25 and Matthew 26:26–28 both tell the words of Jesus at the supper: the bread his body, the cup the covenant in his blood. Paul hands it on as received from the Lord, with the command to do this in memory of him; Matthew has the blood poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Paul's undisputed letters and on Matthew and Mark (dates of writing)

connections.label: Not I, but the Lord
connections.explanation: 1 Corinthians 7:10–11 and Mark 10:9–12 both tell the Lord's command against divorce. Paul marks it as the Lord's word rather than his own, that a wife should not leave her husband nor a husband his wife; Mark gives Jesus' saying that what God has joined no one should separate, and his answer to the disciples in the house.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on Paul's undisputed letters and on Matthew and Mark (dates of writing)

connections.label: Like a thief in the night
connections.explanation: 1 Thessalonians 5:2 and Matthew 24:42–44 both tell that the Lord's coming will be like a thief's, at an hour no one expects. Paul reminds the Thessalonians that they already know the Lord's day will come as a thief does, by night; Matthew gives the saying about the householder who would have watched had he known the hour.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on 1 Thessalonians and on Matthew (dates of writing)

connections.label: I will come as a thief
connections.explanation: 1 Thessalonians 5:2 and Revelation 3:3 both tell that the Lord will come like a thief to those who are not awake. Paul tells the Thessalonians the Lord's day will come as a thief comes, by night; in Revelation the risen Christ warns the church in Sardis that if it does not watch, he will come as a thief at an hour it will not know.

sources.author: Raymond E. Brown
sources.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
sources.locator: the chapters on 1 Thessalonians and on Revelation (dates of writing)

connections.label: Abraham justified by faith, or by works
connections.explanation: Romans 4:1–3 is set against James 2:21–24: both cite the word that Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness. Romans says Abraham was not justified by works, or he would have something to boast of; James says he was justified by works when he offered Isaac, faith working with his deeds. Readers since have weighed how the two fit together.

connections.label: God resists the proud
connections.explanation: James 4:6–10 and 1 Peter 5:5–9 both tell that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble, and call readers to humble themselves before God and resist the devil. James promises that the devil will flee and that God will lift up the humble; First Peter pictures the devil as a roaring lion looking for someone to devour.

connections.label: The image of God, through whom all was made
connections.explanation: Colossians 1:15–17 and Hebrews 1:2–3 both tell of the Son as the image of God through whom all things were made and in whom they hold together. Colossians calls him the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of all creation; Hebrews calls him the radiance of God's glory and the very image of his substance, upholding all things by his word.

connections.label: Coming with the clouds
connections.explanation: Matthew 24:30 and Revelation 1:7 both tell of the Son of Man coming with the clouds and all the tribes of the earth mourning when they see him. Matthew gives it as Jesus' word on the Mount of Olives; Revelation opens with it, adding that those who pierced him will see him.

connections.label: Let your yes be yes
connections.explanation: Matthew 5:34–37 and James 5:12 both tell the command not to swear at all, neither by heaven nor by earth, but to let a yes be yes and a no be no. Matthew gives it in the Sermon on the Mount; James repeats it above all things, so that his readers do not fall under judgement.

connections.label: Blessed when you suffer for righteousness
connections.explanation: Matthew 5:10–12 and 1 Peter 3:14 both tell that those who suffer for righteousness' sake are blessed. Matthew gives it among the Beatitudes, with the promise of the Kingdom; First Peter applies it to believers slandered for doing good, and tells them not to fear what others fear.

connections.label: Subject to the governing authorities
connections.explanation: Romans 13:1–7 and 1 Peter 2:13–17 both tell believers to submit to the governing authorities, who punish wrongdoers and praise those who do good. Romans says every authority is from God and that taxes and honour are owed to whom they are due; First Peter tells readers to honour all people, love the brothers, fear God and honour the king.

connections.label: Our beloved brother Paul
connections.explanation: 2 Peter 3:15–16 names Romans 2:4: Second Peter tells readers to count the Lord's patience as salvation, as Paul wrote in all his letters. Romans speaks in those terms, asking whether the reader despises God's kindness and patience, which lead to repentance. Second Peter adds that some things in Paul's letters are hard to understand, and are twisted by the unstable.

connections.label: The same names in two letters
connections.explanation: Colossians 4:10–14 and Philemon 1:23–24 both tell of the same companions sending greetings with Paul: Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke. Colossians adds that Epaphras wrestles in prayer for them and that Luke is the beloved physician. The shared names tie the two letters to one time and place.

connections.label: Onesimus sent back
connections.explanation: Colossians 4:9 and Philemon 1:10–12 both tell of Onesimus going back to Colossae. Colossians sends him with Tychicus as a faithful and beloved brother who is one of them; Philemon tells his story, a once useless servant who became Paul's child in prison and is now useful, sent back to be received as Paul himself.

connections.label: Jesus Christ come in the flesh
connections.explanation: 1 John 4:2–3 and 2 John 1:7 both tell that whoever does not confess Jesus Christ come in the flesh is not of God, and name that spirit the antichrist. First John gives it as the test of every spirit; Second John warns of many deceivers gone out into the world.

connections.label: Not a new commandment
connections.explanation: 1 John 2:7–8 and 2 John 1:5–6 both tell that the commandment they write is no new one but the one held from the beginning. First John adds that it is new too, since the darkness is passing; Second John says plainly that the commandment is to love one another, and that love is walking in his commandments.

connections.label: Whoever does good is of God
connections.explanation: 1 John 3:10 and 3 John 1:11 both tell that what a person does shows whether he is of God. First John says whoever does not do righteousness or love his brother is not of God; Third John urges Gaius to imitate the good, since whoever does good is of God and whoever does evil has not seen him.

connections.label: What an overseer must be
connections.explanation: 1 Timothy 3:1–7 and Titus 1:5–9 both tell what is asked of an overseer: blameless, the husband of one wife, hospitable, not given to wine, violence or greed, ruling his household well. First Timothy adds that he must not be a new convert; Titus that he must hold to sound teaching, as elders are appointed in every city of Crete.

connections.label: The teaching of Balaam
connections.explanation: Jude 1:11 and Revelation 2:14 both tell of Balaam as the pattern of those who lead God's people astray. Jude sets him beside Cain and Korah as one who erred for reward; in Revelation the risen Christ warns Pergamum about those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to entice Israel to idol feasts and sexual immorality.

connections.label: A new heaven and a new earth
connections.explanation: 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1 both tell of the new heavens and new earth that believers wait for. Second Peter says righteousness dwells there after the present heavens are dissolved; Revelation sees them, the first heaven and earth passed away and the sea no more.

connections.label: Milk, not solid food
connections.explanation: 1 Corinthians 3:1–2 and Hebrews 5:12–14 both tell of believers who still need milk, not solid food. Paul says he could not speak to the Corinthians as spiritual but as infants in Christ; Hebrews says its readers ought to be teachers by now, and that solid food is for the mature, trained to tell good from evil.

connections.label: The voice on the holy mountain
connections.explanation: Matthew 17:1–5 and 2 Peter 1:16–18 both tell of the voice that named Jesus the beloved Son on the mountain. Matthew tells the Transfiguration itself; Second Peter appeals to it as eyewitness testimony, saying that the writer heard the voice from heaven while with him on the holy mountain.

connections.label: Work with your own hands
connections.explanation: 1 Thessalonians 4:11–12 and 2 Thessalonians 3:10–12 both tell the Thessalonians to live quietly and earn their own bread. The first letter asks them to mind their own business and work with their hands; the second recalls the rule that whoever will not work should not eat, and rebukes those who have turned busybodies.
